User: I'm going through a legal process and need to organize my thoughts. The case involves nondisclosure agreement dispute. My lawyer is Lisa Park with Park Legal Group; we have proceedings at the federal district court. We're past the filing stage and waiting for the court calendar.. Opposing party: my former landlord. This is in King County, Washington. The contract was signed last year and they've since stopped performing. Can you help me figure out what to ask my attorney about what documents I should bring and what to say in the hearing? I want to be ready for the legal next steps.
Assistant: I can help — below is a focused, practical plan you can use with your attorney (Lisa Park) to get ready for the next steps in your federal case in King County. I’m not a lawyer, so treat this as organizational and procedural guidance. Confirm strategy and any local rule requirements with Lisa.

First — quick clarifying questions for you (so I can tailor this further):
- Do you know what the next scheduled event will be (e.g., scheduling conference, hearing on a motion, preliminary injunction hearing, status conference, pretrial conference)?  
- Have you done any discovery yet (document production, interrogatories, depositions)?  
- What relief are you asking the court to grant (damages, specific performance, injunction, declaratory relief, attorneys’ fees)?  
Answering those will help me sharpen the list and the suggested hearing statements.

1) Documents and materials to bring to your meeting with Lisa (and to the hearing)
Bring originals if available and well-organized copies (tabbed, with an index). Electronic copies on a USB and a separate cloud link are useful too.

Essential documents:
- The NDA/contract itself (all pages), and any amendments or side agreements.
- Proof of signatures and dates (signed pages, e-sign records).
- All communications with the landlord regarding the NDA and performance (emails, texts, letters, messaging logs)—include dates, senders, recipients.
- Any written demands, notices, or cure letters you sent (and any responses).
- Payment / performance records demonstrating you performed your side (if relevant): invoices, receipts, timelines, work product.
- Documents showing the landlord’s failure to perform (e.g., notices, withheld items, stopped services) and dates when performance stopped.
- Evidence of damages or harm (financial statements, lost business, invoices, receipts, valuation reports, screenshots).
- Any contemporaneous notes you made about events, meetings, phone calls (with dates/time/location).
- Witness contact details and short summaries of what each would testify to.
- Any prior court filings and orders (complaint, service, docket entries, motions, oppositions, court notices).
- Discovery responses (if any): interrogatories, requests for production, responses you gave or received.
- Proposed relief/supporting legal briefs or affidavits (if already prepared).
- Chain-of-custody or metadata evidence for key electronic documents (for authentication).
- A clean chronological timeline (one page or two) of key events (date signed, breach date(s), communications, demands, filings).

Hearing logistics materials:
- Exhibit list (numbered), with a one-line description for each exhibit.
- Multiple paper sets of exhibits (one for judge, one for opposing counsel, one for you, one for your attorney).
- Binder with a “trial/hearing booklet”: timeline, key exhibits tabbed, witness list, short bullet of testimony points.
- USB with scanned exhibits in PDF (labeled and bookmarked).
- A printed one-page summary of what you’ll say (for direct testimony/opening).

2) Questions to ask Lisa Park (use this checklist in your meeting)
Case status and schedule:
- What is the next event on the federal court calendar and what type of hearing will it be?
- Are there local rules, judge-specific standing orders, or required filings I should know (joint status report, proposed scheduling order, pre-hearing statements)?
- What deadlines are coming (initial disclosures, discovery cut-off, motions)?

Evidence & documents:
- Which of the documents I listed are essential vs. merely helpful?
- Do you need originals or certified copies for any items?
- How should electronic evidence be produced and authenticated? Should we preserve metadata?
- Are there particular documents you recommend we obtain now (bank records, logs, communications from the landlord’s side)?

Witnesses & testimony:
- Which witnesses should I expect to call or have called against me? Which should I ask the landlord to call?
- How many witnesses should I plan to bring? Should any give written declarations/affidavits instead?
- Any witnesses we might depose before the hearing?

Legal strategy & briefing:
- What relief are we pursuing and what legal elements must be proven at this hearing?
- What standard will the court apply on our claims (e.g., breach, injunction, irreparable harm, likelihood of success)?
- Should we file any pre-hearing motions (e.g., motion in limine, motion for temporary restraining order, motion for summary judgment)?
- Do you recommend a settlement discussion or mediation now?

Hearing preparation:
- What do you want me to say during the hearing (direct testimony/opening)? Can we script and rehearse it?
- What documents will the court want in advance? Do we need to file an exhibit list or provide courtesy copies?
- Are there special rules for evidence in federal court we should address ahead of time?

Practical & administrative:
- How should I respond to opposing counsel if they contact me directly?
- What should I avoid telling the court or opposing counsel?
- Will you file a proposed scheduling order / joint status report with the court or do you want me to prepare supporting facts?

3) What to say (and how to present) at the hearing — a short script and tips
Opening / short statement to the court (concise, factual, nonargumentative):
- “Good morning, Your Honor. My name is [Your Name]; I’m represented by Attorney Lisa Park of Park Legal Group. This matter concerns enforcement of a nondisclosure agreement signed on [date]. The opposing party, my former landlord, stopped performing under the agreement on [date(s)], despite our written requests to cure. We seek [state relief: e.g., enforcement, injunctive relief, damages]. The key facts are: [one-sentence factual timeline].”

Direct testimony / answering questions:
- Speak calmly, slowly, and stick to facts you personally observed or documents in evidence.
- Use the chronological timeline: signing -> performance -> breach -> notice -> filing -> current status.
- When presenting a document: “This is Exhibit 3; it’s the NDA signed on [date]. I signed it and received it from [who].” Be ready to authenticate (how you received it, where original is).
- Emphasize attempts to resolve (demand letters, emails), since courts like showing parties tried to fix the issue.

If asked by the judge/opposing counsel:
- Answer only the question asked. If unsure, say, “I don’t recall” or “I’ll let my attorney address the legal question.” Don’t speculate.
- If a question requires legal interpretation, defer: “I’ll let Ms. Park address the legal standard.”

Cross-examination preparation:
- Review everything on the record and be consistent with prior statements and documents.
- Don’t volunteer extra information; short, truthful responses are best.
- Prepare for questions about dates, communications, and any inconsistencies — reconcile them ahead of time with Lisa.

4) Evidence & authenticity — practical prep
- Ensure each exhibit has a unique exhibit number and a one-line description.
- Make sure documents have metadata or witness to authentication where possible (who created it, how).
- If emails/texts are critical, print them with headers showing sender/recipient and preserve originals electronically.
- Have a short demonstrative timeline/summary to hand the judge — it helps judges quickly grasp facts.

5) Procedural and local-federal specifics to verify with Lisa
- Confirm judge’s standing orders (some judges require courtesy chambers copies, others want e-filings only).
- Ask about format and timing for exhibit lists and pre-hearing filings in the Western District of Washington.
- Confirm whether the court requires proposed findings, motions in limine, or pre-hearing briefs.
- Ask about whether the court uses any specific exhibit or evidence software (e.g., PDF submissions, ECF procedures for exhibits).

6) Courtroom conduct & logistics
- Arrive early, bring photo ID and your official calendar info.
- Dress conservatively; bring notes, but do not read long statements to the court.
- Bring multiple copies of exhibits (judge, opposing counsel, your binder).
- Coordinate with Lisa about where to sit and when to approach the bench/table.

7) Prepare a one-page summary for Lisa
I recommend preparing a one-page timeline and short witness list to hand Lisa before your next meeting. It should include:
- Key dates (contract signing, breach date(s), demands, filing date).
- 3–5 sentences summarizing the dispute and the relief sought.
- Top 5 documents you consider essential and where they are stored (paper, email folder).
- Names and contact info of any key witnesses.

Would you like me to:
- Draft that one-page timeline and witness list for you to review and give to Lisa?  
- Draft an email to Lisa Park that lists the documents you plan to bring and the questions above (so you can send it in one go)?

Tell me which you prefer and give any details you want included (dates, key documents, relief sought), and I’ll draft it for you.
